blocks.text: At sixteen, Stephanie of Belgium arrived in Vienna to one day become Empress. Eight years later, her husband was dead, her future was destroyed, and at the Viennese court she was treated, as she herself wrote, like a criminal. What happened in those eight years? The marriage began with a shock.

Stephanie had not been prepared for the wedding night at all, and she later recalled it with the harrowing words: “What a night, what agony, what loathing. ” Given that traumatic beginning, one might assume the marriage was doomed from the start. But the story of Rudolf and Stephanie is not that simple. Stephanie at least tried to accept her fate and find happiness.

Shortly after the wedding on the 18th of May, the young couple traveled to Hungary. Already in Pressburg, a triumphal procession began that intensified from station to station. People waited everywhere, flags waved, and again and again Hungarian cheers rang out for the son of Empress Elisabeth, so beloved in Hungary, and for his young wife. Stephanie was overwhelmed. “The reception exceeded everything I had expected. I was intoxicated. All my sorrow seemed to have flown away. I was happy. ”

The Belgian representative, Count de Jong, reported to King Leopold that they had hardly ever experienced a comparable success in Pest. Stephanie’s natural manner, her friendly demeanor, and her smile had earned her great sympathy. At a grand court soiree with over two thousand guests, Stephanie appeared in Hungarian national dress, combined with the jewels the city of Budapest had gifted her for the wedding. The festivities lasted eight days. Knowing of the later catastrophe at Mayerling, it is tempting to view Rudolf and Stephanie’s marriage through the lens of its end, and to see the wedding as the beginning of an inevitable tragedy. But the sources from these first years paint a more nuanced picture. A contemporary report by the Berliner Börsen-Courier noted that while the marriage may not have been born of love, the two young spouses were initially quite fond of each other, and later the marriage even became a quite good one. The princess seemed to gain influence over the prince, and his nature became somewhat calmer. Rudolf’s friend, Count Hoyos, also recalled that the marriage had been a very happy one for a number of years. Rudolf’s own letters are particularly telling. Years after the wedding, he still addressed Stephanie as his dearest angel. In 1885, he wrote to her: “I long for you terribly and am counting the days that still separate us.

” Another time: “My deepest thanks for your telegram. I am quite desperate about this new separation and am already longing for Friday evening. ” He signed it: “Your deeply loving Koco. ” Stephanie, in turn, called him her “cher ami” and signed with the feminine equivalent of his pet name: “Coco-Kokos. ” On December 2nd, 1881, Rudolf wrote to his former tutor, Count Latour: “She is intelligent, very attentive, and sensitive. Full of ambition, a granddaughter of Louis Philippe and a Coburg. I need not say more to you. I am very much in love with her, and she is the only one who could tempt me to do much.

” The later cliché of a boring, unintelligent Stephanie can hardly be reconciled with Rudolf’s own statements from the early years of their marriage. The poor opinion of the Crown Princess actually came from her closest circle—namely, from the Empress. With her wedding, Stephanie had not only become Rudolf’s wife. She was now Crown Princess of Austria-Hungary, the highest-ranking woman at the Viennese court after Empress Elisabeth. One might expect a particularly close relationship between mother-in-law and daughter-in-law. But exactly the opposite was the case. Elisabeth and Stephanie avoided each other whenever possible. The two women were, in many respects, fundamentally different. Stephanie took her position as Crown Princess extremely seriously. She was interested in representation, enjoyed making public appearances, and conscientiously fulfilled the duties associated with her position. Elisabeth, on the other hand, had found those same tasks a burden for years. The strict court ceremonial, receptions, public appearances, and constant observation by society were increasingly hateful to her.

And apparently, the Empress developed an aversion to her daughter-in-law very early on. Elisabeth’s niece, Marie Larisch, recalled an evening walk with the Empress in the autumn of 1882 at Schönbrunn. As they paced up and down in the darkness, the Empress spoke of many things, and also of Rudolf’s marriage, which was already proving to be a failure back then. The evening was quiet, and from the garden they could look over the illuminated windows of the palace. Suddenly a servant hurried toward them and announced the arrival of the Crown Prince and his wife. In the next moment, two silhouettes appeared against the light. Then a figure came down the steps. It was Stephanie. Elisabeth looked toward her intently. “I didn’t expect to see Rudolf and that ugly clumsy oaf again tonight,” Aunt Sissi remarked as she walked across the grass toward her daughter-in-law. The author of the Stephanie biography, Irmgard Schiel, believed one must be cautious with Larisch as a source. Her memoirs were only published decades later, and after this quote appeared in 1913, it was fiercely disputed that Empress Elisabeth could have spoken about her daughter-in-law in such a way.

Such a term, Schiel argued, did not fit the Empress at all. But in the 1980s, well after that biography was published, Elisabeth’s poems were released at the initiative of Brigitte Hamann, confirming Larisch’s statement. In Elisabeth’s poem titled “To Oberrun,” she wrote: “Oberrun, oh, to your right, what a mighty clumsy oaf. Instead of the long false braids, you see blonde fur now here, and it bears pride in its features, even as a clumsy oaf. Folk-dance is its pleasure, the ‘Wibab Salva’ its delight. ” That was not the only poem of this kind. Elisabeth wrote spitefully about her daughter-in-law in her private poetry. This is especially remarkable when one considers that Sisi herself had always found the relationship with her own mother-in-law, Archduchess Sophie, burdensome.

Why did she not try to do better herself? At the time of the wedding, Stephanie was the same age Elisabeth had been, and now she was being mocked by that very woman. Elisabeth also influenced her own daughter Marie with her opinion of Stephanie. Initially, Rudolf’s youngest sister had been quite happy about the new sister-in-law, but that soon changed. Marie Valerie wrote in her diary: “Meanwhile, Rudolf and Stephanie arrived. Papa told me a few days ago that Rudolf does not want to go to the Göding hunt because Stephanie cannot be there. She has actually been going on shooting hunts lately. I think love is the most beautiful thing in the world, but this is ridiculous. ”

She became even clearer in 1882 after a dinner together. Marie Valerie compared Stephanie to her aunt Marie José: “Stephanie was too ridiculous again. She and Rudolf always look at each other, and then she talks as if they had already celebrated their silver wedding anniversary. Aunt Marie José is the exact opposite. Next to her, Stephanie is almost nasty. As I looked at her in her black dress, doe eyes, and cute little face, I wondered if Rudolf didn’t envy Uncle for this lovely woman. Beside her, Stephanie was a hulking figure, so tall, thick, yellow and blonde, and in a hideous white satin dress. How can Rudolf love this cold, mocking, worldly woman so much? Mama fears that instead of being lifted up by him, she is pulling him down to her more and more. ”

On one hand, we see here how Elisabeth transferred her negative image of Stephanie to her daughter. On the other hand, Marie Valerie confirms something quite different almost in passing. Rudolf and Stephanie were apparently very much in love at that time. They were constantly looking at each other. Rudolf even wanted to forgo his hunts if Stephanie could not accompany him. After the wedding, Rudolf and Stephanie spent a long time in Prague, where Rudolf performed his military service. Rudolf was heavily burdened by his military duties and often only returned from the barracks around three in the afternoon. After that, he and Stephanie ate together. Then Rudolf went riding, worked with his staff officers, or devoted himself to his scientific and literary interests. When he worked at home or received guests, he apparently liked having Stephanie nearby. She would sit in the room with needlework or a sketchbook while Rudolf talked with officers, artists, or journalists.

Moritz Szeps, founder and editor-in-chief of the Neues Wiener Tagblatt, who was close friends with Rudolf, reported that Stephanie participated in the conversations and also gave her opinion on political topics. This clearly contradicts the later widespread image of a woman who was mentally uninterested or intellectually inferior to Rudolf. Emotionally, too, the relationship seems to have been much closer during this early marriage than later accounts often suggest. Rudolf even showed signs of jealousy. On the 23rd of February 1882, Stephanie wrote to her sister Louise: “I have noticed that Rudolf did not like seeing me dance with other gentlemen because he is jealous of his little wife. As soon as I saw that and anticipated he might say something to me, I immediately told him I would not dance anymore, so as not to distress him. He was pleased by this and showered me with kindness. When you notice that something displeases your husband, you should stop it immediately, shouldn’t you? ”

For Stephanie, this attitude matched the image of a good wife with which she had grown up. The marriage had absolute priority, and if something bothered Rudolf, she was to forgo it. In her new life, Stephanie was finally able to further develop her own interests, which had not been possible during her childhood. In contrast to Rudolf, she was particularly interested in classical music, opera, theater, and art. Above all, her talent for drawing and painting, which her mother had hardly encouraged, accompanied her throughout her life. When traveling, Stephanie often carried a sketchbook and captured landscapes and places in drawings, and she was apparently quite gifted at it. Two of her drawings of the island of Laoma, today’s Lokrum near Dubrovnik, were later even published in one of Rudolf’s most significant journalistic projects, the so-called “Kronprinzenwerk. ” This monumental project was intended to depict the lands, peoples, landscapes, and cultures of the entire Habsburg Monarchy. Stephanie remained connected to the work even after Rudolf’s death, taking over the later patronage and continuing the enterprise, which grew to a total of twenty-four volumes, until its completion in 1902. Stephanie looked back on the first anniversary of her wedding with particular happiness. She wrote to her sister Louise: “It has been exactly one year since I got married. I can thank God that this first year has passed so well, and I can only pray that the following ones will be just as happy.

Rudi is a real model husband. We get along famously. In a word, dear sister, I am happy. ” Stephanie did not later claim that she had been permanently unhappy from the very beginning. In 1882 she genuinely believed she was in a happy marriage. But something was soon to change, and it would be related to her new duties. On the 28th of October 1881, just half a year after the wedding, Empress Elisabeth summoned her daughter-in-law. Stephanie was to represent her at official occasions in the future.

Elisabeth noted with a certain irony that the Crown Princess had already won all hearts anyway. For the Empress, this was clearly a welcome opportunity, because while Stephanie enjoyed public appearances, Elisabeth had long found the representative duties of her position agonizing. Stephanie later recalled that this slavery, this drudgery, as she called the duties of her position, was hateful to her, and she was of the opinion that freedom was every person’s right. The barely seventeen-year-old Stephanie took on a significant portion of the tasks from which her mother-in-law was increasingly withdrawing. Together with Rudolf, she accompanied the Emperor on his travels. She did the honors when foreign rulers and other high-ranking guests came to Vienna. And she represented Elisabeth at major church ceremonies. These duties also included the Easter ceremonies of the Viennese court. To her sister Louise, she spoke of those magnificent, so uplifting, and only slightly tiring ceremonies. Particularly impressive was the traditional ritual on Maundy Thursday. According to an old court ceremony dating back to Charles V, Emperor Franz Joseph washed the feet of twelve old men from the poorhouse. The Empress had to perform the same task for twelve old women.

But because Elisabeth stayed away from these obligations, Stephanie now had to step in her place. All the ladies-in-waiting appeared in black with long trains and black lace veils. Stephanie had to kneel down in this heavy court attire, pour water from a silver pitcher over the women’s feet, and then dry them with a cloth. And Stephanie could not resist including a little jab at her mother-in-law at this point in her memoirs: “I have never tried to evade these tasks. ” Here the central conflict between Elisabeth and Stephanie becomes apparent. Both women had completely different ideas of what it meant to be a member of the imperial family. Elisabeth perceived representation as a burden. Stephanie perceived it as part of her duty.

Elisabeth sought freedom and withdrew from court as often as possible. Stephanie wanted to fulfill her position and seemed to genuinely enjoy appearing in public as Crown Princess. And it was exactly this that Elisabeth made fun of in her poems about the “clumsy beast. ” What Elisabeth mocked as ridiculous vanity, however, was exactly what was expected of a representative of the monarchy. But the very qualities that made Stephanie suitable for her official role now seemed to start bothering Rudolf. The dignity and seriousness with which she filled her position as Crown Princess appeared increasingly stiff to him. The initial intimacy began to fade, and the differences between them became increasingly apparent. Rudolf was politically restless, liberal, and increasingly critical of the society into which he had been born. Stephanie took dynastic duties and social order extremely seriously. They also differed in their interests. While she loved art, theater, opera, and classical music, hunting played an enormous role for Rudolf. And it was precisely this passion for hunting that would later create more and more distance between him and his family.

As the years passed, the tone of Rudolf’s letters changed. “Dearest angel” first became “dearest Stephanie” and eventually just “dear Stephanie. ” The distance between them grew. Koko and Kokos had become estranged. Stephanie would later summarize this development in one sad sentence: “There was a lack of loving, intellectual unity. It was just living side by side without warmth. ” But in the spring of 1883, a development occurred that brought Rudolf and Stephanie closer together once more. Stephanie was pregnant.

Suddenly, it seemed that what had been expected of her since the wedding might finally come to pass. There were hopes for a future heir to the throne, and Stephanie hoped for a better marriage. “Perhaps,” she hoped, “bonds of affection would form at our child’s cradle that had been denied to our marriage until now. ” For Stephanie, the pregnancy seems to have been a happy time. She and Rudolf grew a little closer again. Rudolf was also looking forward to the baby and adopted a more affectionate tone toward his wife. He wrote to her: “Take very good care of yourself and Watzlaf. ” He thought it would be his son and even called him that: “Be very careful and think of me.

” The birth of the hoped-for heir to the throne was to take place in Laxenburg, where Rudolf himself had been born in 1858. Stephanie was extremely pampered during her pregnancy. Although she was young and healthy, she was soon forbidden from taking long carriage rides. Any physical exertion was to be avoided. Only light walks in the palace park were permitted. Countess de Jong, who visited Stephanie in Laxenburg, found the expectant mother charming, having grown significantly, and much more beautiful and refined than her sister Louise. But she felt sorry for the young Crown Princess because of the restrictions. On the 10th of August 1883, Stephanie’s mother, Marie Henriette, arrived in Laxenburg.

On the 2nd of September, the labor pains began. The birth lasted twenty-six hours, and then the child was finally here. Cannon shots were fired, but not 101, because it was not a successor to the throne. Stephanie later remembered Rudolf’s reaction very clearly. “The Crown Prince’s dismay was painful. My dear mother immediately grasped the embarrassing situation and, with great skill, prevented any reproaches. She handed me my daughter herself, with the words: ‘God bless your child, just as I bless you both with all my heart. ’” On that same day, Empress Elisabeth and Marie Valerie also arrived in Laxenburg.

Marie Valerie noted in her diary that Stephanie was crying because she had only given birth to a daughter. According to her, however, Rudolf supposedly said that it didn’t matter at all, that a daughter is much sweeter after all. But the disappointment of the Belgian family was made clearly palpable. Count Cotteck had already, on the 31st of August, telegraphed Vienna: “King Leopold wishes, in the event of the birth of an Archduke, to attend a Te Deum planned in Brussels. ” After the birth of the daughter, it was merely noted on the telegram: “now moot, filed away. ” The little girl was given the name Elisabeth Marie. Her godmother was her grandmother, Empress Elisabeth, after whom the child was also named. The relationship between Stephanie and her daughter, however, was later judged critically.

Marie Valerie felt Stephanie was not very tender in her dealings with her daughter, and Archduke Karl Ludwig, Franz Joseph’s younger brother and a decided family man, also spoke negatively about it years later. He supposedly said to Count Hübner: “What I do not forgive her for is that she shows no tenderness whatsoever for the little Archduchess Elisabeth, her daughter. ” Here we encounter once again that image of the cold Stephanie, which was repeated so frequently later on. However, one should also be cautious here, because Stephanie had also grown up in a family where tenderness was practically non-existent. Her memories of childhood were marked by distance, discipline, and emotional coldness. In any case, it is certain that Elisabeth Marie would remain the only child of Rudolf and Stephanie. The family life of the Crown Prince couple changed once again when Rudolf was appointed commander of the infantry division and transferred to Vienna. From then on, the family lived in the Vienna Hofburg during the winter months and continued to spend their summers in Laxenburg.

In the Hofburg, the Crown Prince couple moved into rooms in the Swiss Wing, the oldest part of the palace. It was a huge apartment with a 120-square-meter dining hall, called the Hall of Ancestors because of the portraits hanging there. In addition, there was the Turkish salon, a former study, Rudolf’s old bachelor bedroom, the so-called gentleman’s room, a bedroom with a bay window, a library, several cabinets, cloakrooms, salons, and rooms for Stephanie. Later on, separate rooms were also added for Elisabeth Marie. There was also a shared bedroom. Only one thing was missing at first: a bathroom. But as impressive as the size of the Hofburg seemed, Stephanie was by no means enthusiastic about her new home. The living quarters were situated so that many windows looked out onto inner courtyards, and Stephanie was bothered by looking into a courtyard. The kitchen was only a few rooms away, and she complained that the rooms were constantly filled with the smell of food. The rooms were heated with wood, petroleum lamps were used for lighting, and Stephanie was not happy with that either. She complained that these lamps went out after a few hours and spread a foul odor. She wanted to redesign the rooms more tastefully, just as anyone would want to furnish their own home.

But that did not go down well at court at all. The more frequently she addressed grievances, the stronger her reputation as a nagger became. And then, in the eyes of Viennese court society, Stephanie apparently almost committed an affront. She did not like the food at the Hofburg, found the cuisine coarse, and therefore hired a French chef. The young Belgian, who was already considered critical and difficult, was now effectively declaring that the food at the Viennese imperial court was not good enough for her. Stephanie remembered this time: “There was quite a revolution, and unfortunately, family life now began to fall apart increasingly. ” The disappointment over the birth of a daughter had soon led back to the state she already knew from her marriage: a life together that was outwardly correct but inwardly increasingly indifferent. “But our marriage was not actually destroyed even then, for there was still hope. ” Rudolf and Stephanie were young. Theoretically, they still had many years to have a male heir to the throne. But that was exactly what would never happen. In the coming years, not only did Rudolf’s relationship with his wife change, but his lifestyle also became increasingly extravagant.

His affairs increased. And eventually, something happened that took away Stephanie’s chance of ever having another child. In the final years before Rudolf’s death, not much remained of the Crown Prince couple’s initial infatuation. Yet, up until then, there were certainly still happy moments. In 1885, Rudolf and Stephanie took a grand trip to the Orient, which led them as far as Syria. Stephanie later recalled it with enthusiasm: “The magnificent journey is over. It will remain the most beautiful, pleasant memory of my life. We have returned happy. During this time, no clouds had darkened our sky. We were all like one big family and learned to truly respect and know each other. ”

In Abbazia, today’s Opatija, the couple also seemed to have found their way back to each other for a time. Stephanie loved the up-and-coming seaside resort on the Adriatic and stayed there frequently. When Rudolf’s health deteriorated and he longed for warmth, he also went there. But such phases could not hide the fact that the relationship was increasingly falling apart. A decisive point of conflict was Rudolf’s lifestyle. The Crown Prince once even introduced his wife to that world in which he liked to move at night. “Only once did I allow myself to be persuaded to accompany him, disguised as a dashing commoner girl. At first, such an undertaking did not seem without appeal to me. But while I was somewhat astonished at how little the Crown Prince observed the precautions of an incognito, my disappointment was even greater when we visited various café chantants and other questionable establishments in and outside the city together. One sat until dawn at bare, dirty tables.

Beside us, fiacre drivers played cards, whistled, and sang. Girls jumped onto the tables and chairs and sang the same sentimental, vulgar hits over and over. ” What Rudolf apparently perceived as an exciting escape from the rigid courtly world, Stephanie found little appeal in. And these amusements were by no means the biggest problem, for Rudolf had numerous affairs. Meanwhile, at the Viennese court, there was still hope that Stephanie would eventually give birth to a son. But that was never to happen, for in February 1886 Rudolf contracted gonorrhea. At first, Stephanie did not know what her husband was suffering from. “At the beginning of the year, the Crown Prince fell seriously ill.

The doctors, deeply dismayed by the nature of the illness, urged complete rest and isolation. To this end, they recommended a longer stay in the south. We therefore set off immediately for Pula and from there by ship to the pearl of the Adriatic, the magical island of Lokrum located off Ragusa. I was still unclear about the nature of the Crown Prince’s illness. I could only enjoy this wonderful stay for a few days. Then I, too, became seriously ill. For weeks, still unsuspecting, I lay in bed with excruciating pain. Professors from Vienna and Trieste declared that I was suffering from peritonitis. I myself did not suspect the cause of my suffering. By high command, everything was covered up. The doctors were sworn to silence. Only later did I discover and learn that the Crown Prince was to blame for my condition.

” Louise was Stephanie’s only confidante. No one else, not even her parents, suspected the full truth. The illness had devastating consequences for Stephanie. She could not have any more children afterward. With that, the hope for a shared male heir to the throne was finally destroyed. It was especially bitter that, at the Viennese court, it was Stephanie who was later blamed for not having borne Rudolf a son. Looking back, she herself commented on this quite clearly: “The court knew all too well who was at fault for that. ”

From this year on at the latest, six years after the wedding, the marriage seems to have been severely damaged. A contemporary anonymous report claimed that Stephanie had learned of a specific affair of her husband’s at that time and thereafter only wanted to interact with him in the presence of others. Whether the break was actually so clear-cut is hard to say, for even in this phase there are surprisingly intimate letters between the two. Rudolf wrote to his wife, for example: “How I would love to crawl into a good, warm bed with you instead of lying around all alone. ” And even in 1888, a year before his suicide, he wrote: “I think we should sleep together that one night in Abbazia. It would be nice if we could snuggle up to each other in bed again. ”

Apparently, there was no clear, final break in the relationship. Closeness and distance existed side by side. And now, Stephanie increasingly observed a disturbing change in her husband. “Consequently, it happened that the Crown Prince would not return home until early in the morning in an unpleasant state. Under such circumstances, a real life together was no longer possible. My entire being rebelled against it. ” She described Rudolf in the final months of his life not only as becoming increasingly restless and scattered, but also as often letting himself be carried away by the most trivial causes into outbursts of immoderate violence. “His inner turmoil led to terrible outbursts of rage, to unbearable and undignified scenes. It was as if, along with his inner stability, he had also lost all sense of decorum. ”

Yet, on the outside, none of this was to be seen. Stephanie wrote: “The world was not to know anything of the misery into which we had fallen. I was always seen at the Crown Prince’s side. Our joint appearances at the countless occasions that required our presence in the monarchy fortunately left me little time for brooding. ” Publicly, they therefore remained the Crown Princely couple. Privately, they lived increasingly in separate worlds.

And indeed, Stephanie now turned toward another man. In June 1887, the twenty-three-year-old Crown Princess had met Count Arthur Potocki during a trip through Galicia. He was years older than her, a widower, and the father of two daughters. Stephanie fell in love with him. In her secret letters, she called him Hamlet, while she herself became Ophelia. She knew that this relationship could not lead to a happy ending. Her sister Louise was apparently the only person who knew about Stephanie’s feelings and even arranged meetings. In November 1887, Stephanie wrote to Louise: “Hamlet still plays an important role. I cannot forget him. ” And in another letter: “I can no longer bear the restlessness since I know of his presence in Vienna. Ophelia must see him, but how to manage it? Perhaps Rudolf and Fritz are in Abbazia.

Hamlet is only staying in Vienna for two days. Answer immediately with what can be invented. I have already thought about a tour or a dinner with you. Give me some good advice. Try to arrange something. ” How far this relationship actually went cannot be clearly stated from the available sources. But that Stephanie had strong feelings for Potocki is beyond doubt. As late as January 5th, she wrote from Abbazia: “Here the weather is wonderful, the air delicious, the sea superb, life charming, my health restored, the headaches gone, my love for the sea even greater, the temptation to stay in Abbazia has grown.

The fear of returning is terrible! The fondness for this place doubles the longing for Hamlet indescribably. My thoughts and greetings sunk in the waves and my heart is with you. After this litany, you will believe I am starting to lose my mind. ” And in that very January, her husband took a seventeen-year-old girl into his bed and his own life. On the 27th of January 1889, Rudolf appeared at his last public engagement. On the occasion of the birthday of the German Emperor Wilhelm II, the Crown Prince couple attended a reception at the German Ambassador Prince Reuss’s residence. And there was also a young woman present, whose affair with Rudolf had long been talked about in Vienna: Mary Vetsera.

Stephanie’s sister Louise wrote about the situation: “People in Vienna are indeed already talking a lot about Rudolf’s affair with Vetsera. The Crown Princess knows about it, seems to suffer from it greatly, but treats it with silence, in accordance with her noble character. ” Dramatic stories later circulated about a direct confrontation between Mary and Stephanie that evening. Baroness Larisch claimed, for instance, that Mary had refused to perform the required curtsy before the Crown Princess and had demonstratively looked Stephanie in the face. The two women had looked like tigers ready to pounce. However, Larisch herself was not even present that evening, and her spectacular account should not simply be accepted as fact. Stephanie herself mentions nothing of the sort in her memoirs. The report of a man who was actually present at this reception is interesting.

Dr. Konrad Ritter von Zekauer, who wrote under the name Kurt von Zelau: “The tall, slender appearance of Archduchess Stephanie drew everyone’s eyes with her blonde beauty. ” Interesting, given how disparagingly Stephanie’s looks were commented on at her wedding. In the meantime, she was apparently perceived as quite an attractive woman. But Mary also attracted a great deal of attention. Zekauer observed Crown Prince Rudolf speaking with Mary no more or longer than with other young ladies, but their eyes always knew how to find each other. And the situation became particularly striking when it was time to leave. Stephanie had already left the hall and was waiting outside for her husband. However, Rudolf remained behind. Zekauer wrote: “His hesitation to follow his wife, who was already waiting for him in the vestibule, seemed so strange that it had to be noticed by everyone watching the scene. ”

The next day, the 28th of January, Rudolf left for the hunt in Mayerling. Stephanie was not to accompany him. Rudolf had expressly declined her participation. Before he left, Stephanie asked him to stop by their daughter Elisabeth Marie. Stephanie’s lady-in-waiting, Sophie von Planker-Klaps, later remembered this final farewell. Rudolf came to his wife around 11 a. m. in his hunting attire. Upon leaving, Sophie noticed something. Usually, Rudolf said goodbye by saying “Auf Wiedersehen!

”, but on that day, he said: “Farewell! ” Stephanie herself is said to have told her lady-in-waiting afterward: “I have such a strange feeling, as if something is going to happen. ” And then Rudolf drove to Mayerling. He was actually supposed to be back in Vienna the very next day, as a family dinner was scheduled at the Hofburg for the engagement of his sister Marie Valerie. On the 29th of January, Stephanie was just preparing for this dinner when, shortly before 6 p. m. , a telegram arrived from Mayerling: “To Her Imperial and Royal Highness, the most serene Crown Princess Archduchess Stephanie, Vienna. I beg you, write to Papa that I most obediently ask for forgiveness for not being able to appear at the dinner, but because of a bad cold, I would like to forgo the trip this afternoon and stay with Josef Hoyos.

Hugging you warmly, Rudolf. ” It was the last message Stephanie received from her husband. The next day, in the early morning hours of the 30th of January, Rudolf and Mary Vetsera were found dead in Rudolf’s bedroom at Mayerling hunting lodge. Rudolf had killed Mary first and then himself. And with that, Stephanie had become a widow at just twenty-four years old. On that Wednesday morning, Stephanie initially had no idea what had happened in Mayerling. Around ten o’clock, she had her singing lesson as usual. Then, suddenly, her Chief Lady-in-Waiting appeared.

In Stephanie’s memoirs, one can read: “Her expression was unusually serious and closed off when she asked me to follow her, saying she had an important announcement to make. I went with her into the adjoining salon; I looked at her, and even as she spoke cautiously of bad news from Mayerling, I realized that the long-feared catastrophe must have occurred. ‘He is dead,’ I exclaimed. She confirmed it, shaken. ” But Marie Valerie’s diary shows how quickly the question of Stephanie’s complicity arose at court. In it, she writes: “I was then sent to Stephanie to bring her over. Countess Tarouca had told her everything, absolutely everything. Unhappy woman.

She kept begging us all for forgiveness, for she surely felt that her lack of devotion had contributed to driving Rudolf to this horrific act. ” That is, of course, Marie Valerie’s interpretation, but it shows the pressure Stephanie was under immediately after her husband’s death. She had not only suddenly become a widow, but she now had to grapple with the question of whether she would be blamed for her husband’s death. She herself describes the meeting with Emperor Franz Joseph and Empress Elisabeth as follows: “The Emperor was sitting in the middle of the room. The Empress, dressed in dark clothing, snow-white and rigid in the face, was with him. In my stunned, shaken state, I believed they looked at me like a criminal. A crossfire of questions, some of which I could not answer, and others which I was not allowed to answer, rained down on me. ”

In her diary, Stephanie noted on that day: “Appalling news of Rudolf’s death. May God have mercy on the soul of my dearly beloved, precious husband. Peace to his ashes. ” But with her husband, Stephanie had also lost her future. She was no longer the Crown Princess.

At the same time, she had to learn that he had died together with a lover. And now, she was also being blamed for the whole thing. On the same day, she wrote desperately to her sister Louise: “I can barely pick up the pen to tell you how deeply I am wounded by the pain of this terrible misfortune that has befallen us. Come tomorrow, no matter at what hour; I need you more than ever. Pray for me and for him, who was so good. Stay with the unhappiest woman, who is your sister and loves you. ” Louise drove to her immediately, and she recalls: “I composed myself and drove straight to my sister. I found her pale as a corpse and silent.

She held a letter in her hand, the secret of which now belongs to history. ” She means the farewell letter Rudolf had addressed to his wife, in which he wrote: “Dear Stephanie, you are freed from my presence and my burden. Be happy in your own way. Be good to the poor little one, who is all that remains of me. ” Stephanie later commented on this letter in her memoirs: “Every word was like a dagger in my heart. ”

For the Viennese court, however, Rudolf’s suicide posed a religious problem, as a suicide could not be buried in the Catholic Capuchin Crypt. The doctors therefore officially declared that Rudolf had been suffering from mental derangement at the time of his death, allowing him to be buried in the Imperial Crypt. But Stephanie herself did not believe this explanation. She later wrote: “Neither mental derangement, as it was officially claimed later, nor biological flaws inherited from an old dynasty, as some later maintained, were the causes that led to the Crown Prince’s tragic death. I see them solely in the instability of his character. ” On February 2nd, King Leopold and Queen Marie Henriette arrived in Vienna. For once in her life, Stephanie experienced tenderness from her parents.

“In Vienna, we found the Emperor and Empress less ill and shaken than we had expected,” King Leopold wrote to his brother, the Count of Flanders. “We will refrain from describing the despair of our dear Stephanie. The Queen and I spent four full hours with her immediately after our arrival. ” And Stephanie recalls it gratefully: “My mother was full of kindness, understanding, and love. The King, my father, also showed unusual sympathy for me, but he was outraged by the humiliation inflicted upon his daughter, which he felt had tarnished the reputation of his family. ”

Yet, within the imperial family, Stephanie’s behavior was still viewed critically. On the day of Rudolf’s funeral, Marie Valerie observed her sister-in-law closely, and her judgment was once again scathing: “While Mom and I could not hold back our tears, Stephanie spoke coldly and, God forgive me, heartlessly of everything and everyone. Mom said she was ashamed of her in front of the people. When one really gets to know this woman, one must forgive Rudolf for seeking distraction and numbness for his lack of affection elsewhere. Certainly, he would not have become this way if he had had a different wife who understood him. ” These lines clearly show how the image of the supposedly cold, heartless Crown Princess now solidified. Even just days after her husband’s suicide, she was observed mourning, or rather, supposedly not mourning in the right way.

And from this, a judgment was immediately drawn about her marriage and even her complicity in Rudolf’s lifestyle and his affairs. With Rudolf’s death, not only did Stephanie’s marriage change, but the future she had been prepared for since she was fifteen years old suddenly ceased to exist. Her father had declared in Brussels back then that she was destined to become Empress of Austria and Queen of Hungary. For years, Stephanie had lived for this future. She had left her homeland. She had ceremonially submitted to the Viennese court. She had taken on a large portion of the representative duties. She had tried to fulfill the role of a future empress. But now, Rudolf was dead. Stephanie was no longer a future empress. She was the widow of a crown prince whose death had triggered one of the greatest scandals of the Habsburg monarchy. And she was only twenty-four years old.

Yet Stephanie would live for another fifty-six years. She would increasingly distance herself from the Viennese court, fight for her daughter, fall out with Emperor Franz Joseph and her own father, and finally make a decision that, for a Belgian king’s daughter and former crown princess, was tantamount to a social scandal. She would renounce rank, dynastic expectations, and the approval of her family to marry a man she had chosen herself. And the young woman who, at fifteen, hadn’t dared to defy her father’s iron will would eventually become a woman who stood up to that very father.
